paras: The Braggs race riot of May 1903 was an armed confrontation between Black and white residents of Braggs, Indian Territory, eighteen miles northeast of Muskogee, in which a Black man, John Silk, was shot in the back from ambush on May 3. Deputy marshals found the settlement armed but quiet, and on May 5 brought seventeen men, fourteen white and three Black, to Muskogee charged with rioting. An early report of six white men killed ran under the headline "Killed in Race Riot," but later reports named only Silk and a white man, John McBloom, as hurt.

Dispatches said there had been "race trouble" at Braggs for years, and the Butler Weekly Times described a "fierce riot" two months earlier that ended in a pitched battle on the main street. McBloom, who lived four miles from town, had furnished the evidence that sent two Black men, Sam Roach and Jim Taylor, to the penitentiary; on their return, a messenger said, they announced there would be "hell in Braggs before long."

According to that messenger, armed Black men rode into Braggs on Saturday, May 2, and harassed white residents; that night white women and children were taken out of town and an armed band of whites stood guard, the Daily Ardmoreite reported. On Sunday McBloom was fired on by men hidden in his corn crib, whom a Dallas News special called two Black men and the Wichita account supposed were Roach and Taylor. The same day, according to E. B. Smith, who reached Muskogee from Braggs on May 4, Silk was shot in the back from ambush; no report said who shot him.

With the telephone line cut, the marshal's office sent six deputies, and Marshal Bennett promised reinforcements if they did not report by four o'clock on May 4. A messenger that afternoon said the officers had stopped the fighting, though men of both races carried Winchesters and thirty armed Black men had spent the night in a church. He described Silk as "dangerously wounded" and McBloom as not badly hurt.

Deputy Marshal Dave Adams found the place quiet and could not learn who had shot the one man wounded. On May 5 he brought seventeen men charged with rioting to Muskogee; the Plaindealer named them, listing Sam Roach, Richard Parlor and Henry Thompson as the Black prisoners. The Guthrie Daily Leader put the number at twenty, most held on old warrants. The coverage does not show whether Silk survived or how the charges ended.

The story ran on Muskogee wires from May 3 to mid-May in papers from Nebraska and Washington to Georgia and South Carolina. The first reports cast Black residents as the aggressors, as in the Spokane Press headline "Blacks Have Upper Hand in Race War," while Silk's wounding took a single line. The Wichita Daily Eagle, by contrast, headed its fuller account "A Negro Ambushed" and dismissed a similar six-dead claim as the story of a "wildly excited" Black woman.

The arrest wire, which showed most prisoners were white, ran as brief items under headlines such as "Whites and Blacks Not Able To Get Along" in the Atlanta Constitution. The only Black-press report found, a May 15 Plaindealer item, followed that wire's wording, added the prisoners' names, and made no comment.

Casualty accounts differed: one wire reported six whites killed and thirty wounded, a Black woman spoke of a Black man killed by whites and six whites killed, and men who had been at Braggs reported only Silk and McBloom hurt. The cause was given both as the shooting at McBloom and as an attempt to serve warrants on Black residents.

bases: The papers describe a two-sided armed 'race war' at Braggs in which a Black man was shot from ambush, a white man was fired on, both sides armed, and fourteen white and three Black men were arrested for rioting (A1, A7, A9, A20); the type fits loosely (see flags).

Separate Muskogee dispatches, a Dallas News special and a messenger's report carried in the Ardmoreite agree on a riot at Braggs around May 3, the shooting of John Silk, and the arrest of seventeen men (A1, A3, A7, A10, A20); only the casualty count is contested.

framing.detail: Early wires cast Black residents as aggressors ('Blacks Have Upper Hand in Race War', 'the whites are cowed') and gave Silk's shooting a single line, while a Kansas paper headed its version 'A Negro Ambushed.'

The six-dead rumor ran as 'Killed in Race Riot'; the arrest wire ran in the Southeast under 'Whites and Blacks Not Able To Get Along' and 'White and Black Citizens Cannot Live in Peace and Good Will.'
The Plaindealer's 'Territorial Notes' followed the arrest wire's wording, added all seventeen names and that the shooter of the wounded man was unknown, without comment.
